keyTakeaways: The AP called Alaska’s Senate race for Democrat Mary Peltola on Nov. 17, giving Democrats a 56-44 majority after unofficial results showed her ahead of Sen. Dan Sullivan by 12,458 votes.

Peltola is the first Alaska Native elected to the Senate and the first Democrat to win a Senate race in Alaska since 2008, and Alaskans also elected a Democratic governor for the first time since 1998.
Sullivan has not conceded, Alaska is targeting Nov. 25 for certification, and a Justice Department criminal probe and court appeal tied to the ‘other Dan Sullivan’ candidacy remain open.
articles.whyItMatters: The result closes the last Senate contest of the 2026 midterms and widens the Democratic majority that takes office in January. It also leaves a live test of how certification, the Justice Department’s pending appeal and its criminal probe play out after a race in which President Trump personally weighed in.
articles.reportingNote: This source-based news report summarizes public reporting from the Associated Press (via PBS News), Newsweek, CBS News, the Alaska Beacon, Democracy Docket and Al Jazeera available as of Nov. 19, 2026. Vote totals are unofficial results reported by Newsweek from the Alaska Division of Elections. The figure of more than 200 subpoenas comes from a Fox News Digital report that Newsweek said it had not independently confirmed. Democracy Docket’s founder, Marc Elias, leads the law firm that represents Peltola’s campaign, so we use its reporting only for court and procedural details. Peltola, the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. deny coordinating, and no charges have been announced. Details may change as officials and courts act.

articles.title: Peltola Wins Alaska Senate Race, Lifting Democrats to 56 Seats
articles.subtitle: Sen. Dan Sullivan has not conceded, and a Justice Department probe into the ‘other Dan Sullivan’ candidacy continues as Alaska targets Nov. 25 for certification
articles.excerpt: Democrat Mary Peltola defeated Sen. Dan Sullivan, according to the Associated Press, flipping Alaska’s seat and giving Democrats a 56-44 Senate majority. Sullivan has not conceded, certification is targeted for Nov. 25, and a Justice Department probe into the ‘other Dan Sullivan’ candidacy continues.

toc.text: The count and what it means

content.text: Democrat Mary Peltola has defeated Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, winning the last U.S. Senate race left undecided from the Nov. 3 midterms and lifting Democrats to a 56-44 majority in the chamber, according to the Associated Press. The AP called the contest at 10:19 p.m. Eastern on Tuesday, Nov. 17, two weeks after Election Day, shortly after officials confirmed she had topped 50 percent of the first-choice vote, so no ranked-choice runoff was needed.

The result is not final. Alaska is aiming to certify it on Nov. 25, Sullivan has not conceded, and a Justice Department criminal investigation into how a second candidate named Dan Sullivan reached the ballot is still running, Newsweek reported.
The count and what it means

Unofficial results from the Alaska Division of Elections, as reported by Newsweek, showed Peltola with 144,302 votes (50.12 percent) and Sullivan with 131,844 (45.80 percent). Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired Petersburg teacher who appeared on the ballot with no party label, received 4,760 votes (1.65 percent). Peltola’s lead of 12,458 votes is larger than his entire total, a point Newsweek highlighted because the Justice Department’s lawsuit rested on the idea that votes for him might otherwise have gone to the incumbent.

CBS News reported that Peltola is the first Alaska Native elected to the Senate and the first Democrat to win a Senate race in the state since 2008. The AP noted she will be only the fifth Democrat since statehood to represent Alaska in the chamber; the last was Mark Begich, whom Sullivan defeated in 2014. Al Jazeera observed that her win does not decide which party controls the Senate, since Democrats already had enough seats, but it widens their majority. The AP said Democrats flipped nine Republican-held seats overall, including in conservative states such as South Carolina, Texas, Kansas and Mississippi.
How Peltola won

Peltola, who is Yup’ik, was the first Alaska Native to serve in Congress. She lost her House seat to Republican Nick Begich in 2024 and then became central to Democratic plans to retake the Senate, the AP reported. She finished first in the August open primary with 49.5 percent to Sullivan’s 41.4 percent.

In the general election she ran an Alaska-first campaign built around fuel prices, housing and the cost of food and supplies in remote communities, and she tried to keep her distance from national Democrats. Sullivan’s campaign sought to link her to liberal priorities in the Lower 48 that it said would restrict oil, gas and mining development. Peltola said she would work with President Donald Trump where it helped Alaska, and after the call she said the result showed Alaskans want change from business as usual in Washington, according to the AP.

Alaskans also elected Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins governor, the party’s first win for that office since 1998, and voters rejected a ballot measure to repeal the state’s open primaries and ranked-choice system, the AP reported. As of Nov. 18 the AP had not called the U.S. House race between Republican Rep. Nick Begich and independent Bill Hill.
The ‘other Dan Sullivan’ dispute

The final weeks of the race were dominated by Sullivan Jr.’s candidacy. Less than a week before Election Day, The New York Times reported that people connected to Peltola’s campaign had helped try to recruit a candidate who shares the incumbent’s name. The AP said the report drew on text messages, documents and interviews with a former campaign manager who was fired before the primary and later sought to retract her statements. Trump called for Peltola to be prosecuted.

Peltola says she knew nothing about other candidates on the ballot, and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee denies involvement. Sullivan Jr. has said he had no contact with her campaign, and Newsweek noted he has long maintained that running was his own idea. Democracy Docket, whose founder’s law firm represents Peltola’s campaign, argued that political groups working with other candidates to draw votes from a rival is neither unusual nor illegal. The Justice Department has not said which federal laws it believes may have been broken.
Legal fights still open

The Justice Department sued Alaska on Oct. 22 to block certification if Sullivan lost, and Trump has said he ordered the suit. U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason dismissed it on Nov. 1, finding the government lacked standing and that setting aside ballots would violate ballot secrecy, Newsweek reported. The department appealed to the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, where voting-rights groups have asked the court to uphold the ruling without full briefing, a motion that pauses the department’s Dec. 14 brief deadline. UCLA election-law scholar Richard Hasen wrote that he would not be surprised if the department dropped the appeal, and a response to that request was due Nov. 19. Separately, an Alaska attorney has asked Gleason to sanction three Justice Department lawyers who brought the suit.

On the criminal side, Fox News Digital reported, citing a law enforcement source, that prosecutors have issued more than 200 subpoenas in an investigation reaching several states with more than one target. Newsweek said it had not independently confirmed that figure. The AP earlier reported that target letters went to several people, including Democratic election lawyer Marc Elias, whose firm represents Peltola’s campaign; Elias has said he is being targeted. Newsweek also relayed the AP’s observation that the administration has had repeated trouble getting grand juries to indict in politically charged cases. A state inquiry opened at Gov. Mike Dunleavy’s direction also continues, Alaska’s public safety department told Newsweek.
What comes next

Alaska’s elections division has targeted Nov. 25 to certify the result after review by the State Review Board, and Nov. 30 is the last day to request a recount in the Senate race and most other contests, Newsweek reported. Under Alaska law, a challenger can file an election contest once state review is complete, according to Democracy Docket. Sullivan’s campaign has said it will let the process run until every legal vote is counted and certified, and it has not conceded.

Trump has called the contest rigged and demanded that votes cast for Sullivan Jr. be awarded to the incumbent, Newsweek and Democracy Docket reported, and Democracy Docket said some congressional Republicans have questioned whether Peltola would be seated. Dunleavy, who has not committed to certifying a Peltola win, is set to leave office Dec. 7 and is expected to be succeeded by Kreiss-Tomkins. The key open questions are whether certification happens on schedule, whether the Justice Department keeps pursuing its appeal and criminal probe, and what happens when the Senate convenes in January. Details may change as officials and courts act.

keyTakeaways: White House counsel Will Scharf warned incoming House Oversight Chair Robert Garcia in a Nov. 9 letter that threats against officials, or process meant only to instill fear, could cross into criminal territory.

U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz told Sen. Richard Blumenthal to preserve ballroom-inquiry records and confirm by Nov. 18, while Attorney General Todd Blanche said no criminal investigations of incoming members are open.

articles.whyItMatters: Congressional oversight is one of the few formal checks on a president, and how hard each side tests its limits will shape the final two years of Trump’s term. The administration says it is defending officials from abuse of subpoena power, while Democrats say framing oversight as a legal risk is meant to deter people from cooperating.

articles.title: White House and DOJ Warn Democrats That Oversight Probes Could Be Criminal
articles.subtitle: The administration’s letters to Rep. Robert Garcia and Sen. Richard Blumenthal open a legal fight before Democrats take over congressional committees in January
articles.excerpt: White House counsel Will Scharf told incoming Oversight Chair Robert Garcia that threats against officials and subpoenas meant to instill fear could cross into “blatant criminality,” and a U.S. attorney sent Sen. Richard Blumenthal a similar warning. Attorney General Todd Blanche says no criminal probes of incoming members are open.

content.text: White House counsel Will Scharf has warned the California Democrat who will lead the House Oversight Committee that threats against administration officials, or subpoenas meant only to instill fear, could cross into “blatant criminality,” escalating a confrontation that began within days of the Nov. 3 midterms. In a letter to Rep. Robert Garcia dated Nov. 9 and made public on Nov. 11, Scharf argued that congressional subpoenas must serve a legitimate legislative purpose and added that issuing unlawful ones to deprive people of their rights could warrant further investigation.

The same day the letter became public, Aaron Reitz, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, sent a related warning to Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, telling him to preserve records tied to his inquiry into donors to the White House ballroom. Attorney General Todd Blanche has since said no criminal investigations of incoming members of Congress are open over their oversight-related comments, and Democrats say they will not be deterred.
What the Scharf letter says

Scharf wrote that Congress’s compulsory process is available for oversight functions and only for them, and cannot be used to exercise prosecutorial power that belongs to the executive and judicial branches. He cited two Supreme Court decisions, Watkins v. United States from 1954 and Trump v. Mazars from 2020, which limit committee demands for testimony and for private records, according to ABC News.

The letter points to recent Democratic comments as evidence of improper motives. They include Garcia’s election-night post telling administration officials to “lawyer up” and social media posts by Reps. Emily Randall of Washington and Analilia Mejia of New Jersey joking about handing out subpoenas freely, according to ABC News and USA Today. ABC News noted it is unclear how any of the cited statements could implicate federal criminal law, since lawmakers have sweeping protection under the Constitution’s Speech or Debate Clause and the Supreme Court has set a very high bar for what counts as a true threat.
The Justice Department’s parallel warnings

Blumenthal is set to chair the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations. In October he wrote to more than a dozen donors named in Washington Post reporting on the ballroom’s funding, asking what they had given and received. Reitz accused him of threatening supporters of President Donald Trump and asked him to confirm by Nov. 18 that he was preserving the related records. Politico noted that the White House and Justice Department letters both borrow language from a federal conspiracy-against-rights statute. Reitz’s letter did not say Blumenthal is under criminal investigation, and Blumenthal called the implied threat baseless and sent Reitz a letter of his own directing him to preserve his communications about it. Politico reported that Reitz sent a similar letter to Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan on Thursday.

Blanche has been less categorical than the letters. On CNN on Sunday, Nov. 8, he left open the possibility that Democratic rhetoric could be criminal, saying it depended on what was said. At a news conference Thursday, he said there were no active criminal investigations of incoming members over their comments and that he had not determined any criminal line had been crossed, Politico reported.
How the administration is preparing

Politico reported, citing The Washington Post, that Scharf has added 15 lawyers to the White House counsel’s office, which has been meeting with agency officials to plan responses to congressional demands. It also noted that the Justice Department issued an opinion in August extending executive privilege to communications with private advisers outside government, a position Democrats have called an attempt to shield witnesses before investigations begin.

The legal warnings are paired with a political message casting Democrats as the corrupt party. White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said Trump has launched an all-out war on fraud across the federal government, and Politico reported that Republicans’ early goal is to portray the new majority as spending its time on vengeance rather than lowering costs. Politico added that the threat of prosecution is not hypothetical for Democrats: a grand jury declined in February to indict six Democratic lawmakers over a video urging troops to disregard unlawful orders, and federal agents raided Rep. Ilhan Omar’s Washington home in October in an immigration-related inquiry she has called political retaliation.
How Democrats are responding

Garcia answered that Congress’s investigative power comes from Article I of the Constitution rather than the White House’s permission, and said the letter suggested Trump has something to hide. Democrats have signaled possible investigations into Elon Musk, the Trump family’s crypto ventures, the ballroom and other White House projects, the Iran war and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, USA Today reported. Garcia has told CNN he is prepared to go to court if the White House refuses to comply with subpoenas, The Hill reported, and Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland, expected to chair the Judiciary Committee, said Garcia would be within bounds to seek a restraining order. Court action matters because criminal contempt referrals would go to Blanche’s own department, where, the Associated Press noted, they would almost certainly not be acted on.

Legal views are mixed on the tactic. David Rapallo, a Georgetown law professor and former Oversight Committee staff director under Democratic Chair Elijah Cummings, called it “a little ridiculous” given the Constitution’s text but said it could still chill non-elected people who might cooperate with investigators, Politico reported. Will Chamberlain of the Trump-aligned Article III Project told Politico that Justice Department prosecutions will keep serving as the administration’s own counter-messaging. Scharf, defending the letter on Newsmax, said Congress cannot investigate for the purpose of inflicting pain on officials, The Hill reported.
What comes next

The first fixed date is Nov. 18, when Reitz wants Blumenthal to confirm he is preserving records. Democrats cannot compel testimony or documents until they take committee gavels in January; until then, Blumenthal can ask donors for information but cannot force them to reply, the International Business Times reported. Open questions include whether the Justice Department opens any inquiry into members of Congress, how broadly the White House asserts executive privilege, and how courts handle the first subpoena disputes. Details may change as officials and lawmakers respond.

articles.title: Bessent Blames Commerce for Megaspeed Blacklist Delay as Lutnick Agrees to Testify
articles.subtitle: The Treasury secretary’s public rebuke, a reported White House debate over Lutnick’s future and bipartisan demands for answers put Commerce’s China chip policy under scrutiny
articles.excerpt: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Commerce “has the pen” on export blacklists, a day after Reuters reported White House officials were discussing Howard Lutnick’s future and as Lutnick agreed to testify to the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 10.

toc.text: Why Megaspeed is at the center

content.text: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has publicly pointed to the Commerce Department for the Trump administration’s failure to blacklist Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based buyer of Nvidia chips that U.S. officials suspect of routing advanced processors to China. Speaking on CNBC on Friday, Bessent said Treasury, the Pentagon, the U.S. Trade Representative and the State Department had favored adding the company to the Entity List for months, but that Commerce “has the pen.”

The remarks came one day after Reuters reported that senior White House officials were discussing whether Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick should be pushed out, and on the same day CBS News reported that Lutnick had agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 10, according to a U.S. official. A White House official has said President Donald Trump “maintains complete confidence” in Lutnick, and no decision to remove him has been announced.
What Bessent said

Asked on CNBC’s Squawk Box about reported tension between him and Lutnick, Bessent declined to discuss those reports but made the division of responsibility plain. The Entity List, which restricts which foreign companies can receive sensitive U.S. technology, is administered by Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security. Other agencies could push for a listing, he said, but the decision sits with Commerce, and questions about its internal process should go there.

Axios reported on Wednesday that Bessent confronted Lutnick in a White House Situation Room meeting after the Nov. 3 midterms, asking why Megaspeed had not been listed. According to Axios, Lutnick answered that he would look into it. A Commerce Department spokesperson told Axios the account was false and that the two secretaries had no such conversation.

Axios also noted that the rivalry between the two men dates to Trump’s transition, when both sought the Treasury job, and that Commerce has not added a single company to the Entity List in more than a year, based on a review of the Federal Register.
Why Megaspeed is at the center

Reuters reported that Megaspeed has bought more than $4.8 billion in advanced Nvidia AI chips since June 2024. The U.S. government suspects the company of directing advanced chips to China in a way that circumvents American export restrictions. Megaspeed has said it is a compliant and legal company, and China’s Foreign Ministry has dismissed the espionage allegations as groundless, according to CNN as relayed by Newsweek.

The scrutiny intensified after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned on Nov. 12, effective immediately. Four days earlier, Huang had told employees in a message that he had an extramarital affair, and Nvidia’s board had announced an independent investigation amid reports that he was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. The relationship was with Alice Huang, who is not related to him and previously led Megaspeed. U.S. officials suspect her of passing information to Beijing, according to reporting by The New York Times summarized by CBS News. The reporting describes suspicion, and this article does not treat it as proven.
The New York Times has also reported that Commerce Undersecretary Jeffrey Kessler abruptly halted a Megaspeed investigation after Nvidia intervened, according to Axios’s account of that reporting.
Pressure from both parties

Republicans have been among the sharpest critics. Sen. Jim Banks of Indiana, a Banking Committee member, said Commerce appeared to have used loopholes to allow chip sales that Trump had directed the department not to permit. Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana told Politico that Lutnick should explain his choices publicly. Asked on CNN whether Lutnick should lose his job, Kennedy said he did not know yet. Rep. Bill Huizenga of Michigan said Commerce had not been responsive to lawmakers, while Rep. Brian Mast of Florida said he has confidence in Lutnick but wants Congress to examine how the department approves chip exports.

Democrats, who won control of Congress in the midterms and take over in January, are seeking records. Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons asked Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller to preserve documents on Nvidia’s advanced chip exports to China. Warren is set to chair the Senate Banking Committee next year. Sen. Ron Wyden and Rep. Richard Neal said they are investigating the administration’s approval of chip sales to Chinese companies with troubling ties, and they described the December 2025 arrangement that allowed Nvidia H200 sales to China in exchange for a share of revenue as an “unconstitutional export tax.”
What comes next

The Dec. 10 Banking Committee appearance is the next fixed date. Lutnick is likely to face questions about the Entity List freeze that began in October 2025, the reported halt of the Megaspeed inquiry and what he told colleagues. Reuters has reported that the administration also held off blacklisting Chinese AI startup DeepSeek, memory chipmaker CXMT and more than 100 other companies flagged as potential national security risks, amid concerns about tensions with Beijing.

The White House has so far stood by Lutnick publicly. Separately, CBS News’s timeline notes that Trump said on Nov. 9 he learned of the allegations surrounding Huang’s relationship only recently. Whether that public support holds as Republican criticism grows and Democrats prepare investigations is the main open question. Reporting on the internal White House discussions relies on anonymous sources, and details may change as officials respond.

keyTakeaways: The Supreme Court lifted a lower-court ban on third-country deportations.
Full arguments on the policy are scheduled for December.
The ruling is expected to speed removals in the weeks before the midterms.
articles.whyItMatters: The decision temporarily restores a key enforcement tool and sets up a major immigration case for the term that begins in October.
articles.reportingNote: This report is based on public statements, court filings and contemporaneous coverage of the events described.
articles.title: Supreme Court clears path for third-country deportations, for now
articles.subtitle: The justices granted an emergency request while scheduling fuller arguments later this year
articles.excerpt: The Supreme Court on Tuesday allowed the administration to resume rapid deportations of migrants to countries that are not their own, overturning a lower-court ban while agreeing to hear arguments on the policy in December.

toc.text: What it means on the ground

content.text: The Supreme Court on Tuesday cleared the way for the Trump administration to resume deporting migrants to third countries that are not their nations of origin, granting an emergency request that overturned a lower-court injunction blocking the practice.

In a brief unsigned order, the justices said the administration may continue the policy for now. The court also scheduled oral arguments for December on whether the policy is lawful under immigration statutes and the Constitution.
What the order does

Under the challenged approach, immigration authorities can remove people to a country other than the one they left, including nations with which the United States has bilateral removal agreements. Advocates had argued that such removals can strand people in places where they face persecution or lack basic protections.

A federal district judge had blocked the rapid third-country transfers earlier this year, finding that the government had not adequately considered individual safety claims. An appeals court left that injunction largely in place, prompting the emergency application to the Supreme Court.
The legal fight ahead

The December arguments will focus on statutory authority for third-country removals and on due-process claims raised by the challengers. Immigration lawyers say the outcome could reshape how the government manages removals when home-country repatriation is delayed or blocked.

The administration has argued that third-country options are essential to enforce immigration law when origin countries refuse to accept returnees. Civil-rights groups counter that the speed of the process leaves too little time for people to raise credible-fear claims.
What it means on the ground

With the midterm elections weeks away, the order is likely to accelerate removals that had been paused. Border and interior enforcement agencies had already expanded capacity for transfers; the ruling removes the main judicial barrier that had slowed those plans.

State attorneys general on both sides of the immigration debate are preparing follow-on litigation. Several blue-state officials said they will continue to challenge individual transfers they view as unsafe, while several red-state officials welcomed the ruling as restoring enforcement tools.

keyTakeaways: A $15 billion steel mill is planned for Iowa with a 2030 production target.
Officials project up to 1,750 permanent jobs.
The announcement comes weeks before the November midterms.
articles.whyItMatters: Large industrial projects are a central campaign theme; this one gives the administration a concrete Midwest manufacturing story.
articles.reportingNote: This report is based on public statements, court filings and contemporaneous coverage of the events described.
articles.title: Trump announces $15 billion steel plant in Iowa ahead of midterms
articles.subtitle: The project is pitched as creating up to 1,750 permanent jobs and boosting domestic steel capacity
articles.excerpt: President Trump announced plans for a $15 billion steel mill in Iowa, describing it as among the largest in the country and tying the project to a broader push for domestic manufacturing before the November elections.

content.text: President Trump on Monday announced a plan for a $15 billion steel mill in Iowa, presenting the project as a major expansion of domestic steel capacity and a jobs win for a key Midwest state weeks before the midterm elections.

Speaking at the White House alongside company executives and state officials, Trump said the facility, to be built by Mesabi Metallics, would rank among the largest steel plants in the United States and would support a wider effort to reduce reliance on foreign steel.
The announcement

White House officials said the plant is designed to produce about 10 million tons of steel a year. The company aims to begin production by 2030. Details on site selection within Iowa and on any federal financing or tax incentives were not fully spelled out at the announcement.

Mesabi Metallics has been developing iron-ore and steel projects for years. The Iowa announcement is the most concrete public commitment yet to a full-scale mill of this size under the current administration.
Jobs and timeline

Officials projected as many as 1,750 permanent jobs once the plant is operating, plus thousands of construction positions during the build-out. State economic-development agencies are expected to negotiate local incentives in the coming months.

Industry analysts noted that global steel markets remain competitive and that long lead times for permits, power supply and skilled labor could stretch the 2030 target. The administration framed the project as part of a broader industrial policy that also includes tariffs and Buy American rules.
Political context

The timing is deliberate. Iowa is not a traditional steel stronghold, but the announcement gives Republicans a positive manufacturing message in a region where factory jobs remain a potent campaign theme. Democratic critics said the project is years away from producing steel and does little for workers facing near-term layoffs or plant closures elsewhere.
Trump also used the event to answer questions on Iran policy and the midterms, tying economic announcements to a wider argument that his administration is delivering tangible industrial results.

keyTakeaways: Army Secretary Daniel Driscoll is resigning after reported tensions with Defense Secretary Hegseth.
An acting secretary is expected to be named quickly.
The move comes while the Army supports operations in multiple theaters.
articles.whyItMatters: Civilian leadership continuity at the Army matters for readiness and for congressional oversight of a force stretched across major conflicts.
articles.reportingNote: This report is based on public statements, court filings and contemporaneous coverage of the events described.
articles.title: Army Secretary Driscoll resigns after reported tensions with Hegseth
articles.subtitle: The departure leaves the Army leadership transition incomplete as the military manages two major overseas conflicts
articles.excerpt: U.S. Army Secretary Daniel P. Driscoll is stepping down after months of reported friction with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, according to the White House and people familiar with the decision.

content.text: Army Secretary Daniel P. Driscoll is resigning after roughly 18 months in the job, the White House confirmed, following months of reported tension with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over priorities, personnel and the Army's role in ongoing conflicts.

Driscoll submitted his resignation effective in the coming days. Neither the White House nor the Pentagon detailed a specific policy dispute, but multiple people familiar with the situation said the relationship had deteriorated over the summer as the Army balanced demands from the Iran theater and other global commitments.
The resignation

Driscoll had been viewed as a relatively low-profile manager of the Army's day-to-day affairs. His departure is the highest-level civilian change at the service this year and comes as the Pentagon works through a broader leadership reshuffle.
Defense officials said an acting secretary will be named quickly. Confirmation of a permanent replacement could stretch into the post-midterm period depending on the Senate calendar.
Context of two wars

The Army is supporting operations tied to the prolonged conflict with Iran and continues to maintain force posture in Europe and the Indo-Pacific. Senior officers have warned that extended large-scale operations in the Middle East risk reducing readiness for other contingencies.

Those readiness concerns formed part of the background to the reported friction between the Army secretariat and the Office of the Secretary of Defense, according to people briefed on internal discussions.
What comes next

Lawmakers on the House and Senate Armed Services Committees said they expect a full briefing on the transition. Some members privately expressed concern that repeated civilian turnover at the services complicates oversight of procurement and force-structure decisions.
The White House framed the change as a routine personnel move and said it remains committed to supporting the Army's missions abroad.

keyTakeaways: A federal judge blocked key parts of new federal mail-in voting restrictions.
The order sits alongside earlier Supreme Court action that allowed other pieces of the policy.
State election officials are navigating conflicting guidance weeks before ballots go out.
articles.whyItMatters: Mail ballots are a large share of the vote in many states; last-minute federal rule changes create operational and legal risk for election administrators.
articles.reportingNote: This report is based on public statements, court filings and contemporaneous coverage of the events described.
articles.title: Judge issues new block on sweeping mail-in voting restrictions
articles.subtitle: The ruling is the latest turn in a fast-moving legal fight over election rules before the midterms
articles.excerpt: A federal judge issued a fresh injunction limiting the administration's effort to restrict mail-in voting nationwide, even as earlier Supreme Court action had cleared a path for parts of the same agenda.

content.text: A federal judge on Thursday issued a new block on key pieces of the Trump administration's effort to restrict mail-in voting, finding that the latest rules risked disenfranchising eligible voters without clear statutory authority.

The order does not reverse every prior appellate or Supreme Court step in the long-running dispute, but it freezes specific federal directives that states and the Postal Service had begun to implement.
The ruling

Judge Indira Talwani wrote that the Postal Service appeared to be carrying out a "haphazard experiment" with procedures that could produce "major disenfranchisement" if left unchecked before ballots are mailed in large numbers.

The administration has argued that the changes are needed to reduce fraud and to align federal practice with state deadlines. Voting-rights groups and several state election officials countered that the rules would force premature rejection of ballots that arrive after arbitrary cutoffs.
Competing court orders

Earlier this summer the Supreme Court allowed parts of a related executive order to take effect while litigation continued. That decision left room for as-applied challenges, which is the path the latest district-court injunction followed.
Election lawyers say the patchwork of orders will force state officials to track multiple federal directives at once as they prepare for early voting and mail ballot distribution.
State response

Secretaries of state in several battleground jurisdictions said they will follow the newest injunction while seeking clarification from the Justice Department. Private voting-rights attorneys and Democratic attorneys general are preparing additional suits if further federal guidance is issued before Election Day.
Republican state officials who support tighter mail rules said they will continue to press for higher verification standards under state law regardless of the federal outcome.

keyTakeaways: A State Department watchdog says VOA cuts damaged U.S. national interests.
The report cites lost language services and correspondent capacity.
Lawmakers in both parties are pressing for partial restoration of services.
articles.whyItMatters: International broadcasting is a long-standing tool of U.S. public diplomacy; the inspector general's findings reopen the debate over how much capacity to maintain.
articles.reportingNote: This report is based on public statements, court filings and contemporaneous coverage of the events described.
articles.title: Voice of America cuts hurt U.S. national interests, internal watchdog says
articles.subtitle: A State Department inspector general assessment echoes bipartisan criticism of the decision to shutter VOA services
articles.excerpt: An internal State Department watchdog concluded that reductions to Voice of America programming damaged U.S. national interests, adding to criticism from lawmakers in both parties of the decision to scale back the broadcaster.

content.text: The State Department's inspector general has concluded that cuts to Voice of America programming harmed U.S. national interests, according to an assessment that tracks closely with warnings raised by critics of the decision to shutter or sharply reduce VOA services.

The report does not call for an immediate reversal of every reduction, but it finds that the loss of language services and correspondent capacity weakened the ability of the United States to counter foreign propaganda and to reach audiences in contested information environments.
The findings

Inspectors reviewed the wind-down of several language services and the reassignment or departure of experienced journalists. They found gaps in coverage of regions where state-controlled media dominate the information space and where U.S. messaging had previously maintained a steady audience.
The assessment notes that some savings were real but that the strategic cost of reduced reach was not fully weighed in the original decision documents.
Congressional reaction

Several Republicans who have long supported international broadcasting joined Democrats in citing the inspector general's conclusions. Members of the foreign-affairs committees said they will press for a detailed plan to restore priority language services.

Administration officials defended the original cuts as necessary fiscal discipline and said remaining platforms still deliver core messaging. They have not committed to reversing the largest reductions.
What remains

Voice of America continues limited English and selected language programming. Partner networks and digital products carry some of the load, but the inspector general found that those substitutes do not fully replace the lost correspondent capacity or the brand recognition VOA had built over decades.
Further oversight hearings are expected this fall as appropriators weigh whether to restore funding in the next budget cycle.

articles.author: admin
keyTakeaways: California banned shock gloves and similar devices for immigration officers.
A new tax targets certain private detention facilities.
Federal legal challenges are possible as the state asserts greater oversight.
articles.whyItMatters: State limits on immigration enforcement tools and facilities are a growing front in the federalism fight over immigration policy.
articles.reportingNote: This report is based on public statements, court filings and contemporaneous coverage of the events described.
articles.title: Newsom signs California laws targeting ICE detention practices
articles.subtitle: The measures include a ban on shock devices and a new tax on certain detention facilities
articles.excerpt: California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a package of bills aimed at Immigration and Customs Enforcement practices, including a ban on shock gloves and a tax on detention centers, after reports that ICE planned to purchase stun devices for officers.

content.text: Gov. Gavin Newsom signed legislation this week that bans shock gloves and similar stun devices for use by immigration officers in California and imposes a new tax on certain private detention centers used by Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Democrats in Sacramento moved the package after reports that ICE was exploring purchases of shock devices for field officers. The bills also expand state oversight of conditions inside facilities that house immigration detainees.
The bills

One measure prohibits the sale and use of specified electroshock gloves and related devices by immigration enforcement personnel operating in the state. Another creates a detention-center tax intended to discourage expansion of private facilities under state jurisdiction.

Supporters said the laws respond to documented injuries and to community opposition to expanded detention capacity. Opponents argued that the measures interfere with federal authority and could make it harder to hold people subject to removal orders.
Federal response

Federal officials have previously challenged state limits on cooperation with ICE and are expected to review whether the new tax and device ban conflict with federal supremacy principles. No lawsuit had been filed at the time of the signing.
ICE has not publicly detailed any finalized purchase of shock gloves. The agency has said it continuously evaluates equipment for officer safety and for compliance with use-of-force policy.
National debate

California's package is the latest in a series of state-level efforts to regulate the tools and facilities used in immigration enforcement. Similar debates are underway in other large states over local cooperation, data sharing and the siting of detention centers.

The midterm campaign has elevated immigration enforcement as a national issue; state actions like California's ensure the fight will continue in legislatures and courts regardless of the November results.
